utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, kindly call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Today is Tuesday, the 6th of May. My greetings to the Prosecution, the Defence counsel, the accused, and everyone helping us. Today, we are going to continue with Mr. Prlic's opening statement. He has the floor. THE ACCUSED PRLIC: Thank you, Mr. President. [Interpretation] In light of the allegations in the indictment related to inter alia the functioning of the prisons, let me say that apart from the district prison in Mostar, as indicated in the report issued by the Department for Judiciary and General Administration, page 57, and now I quote: "So far district, military, and civilian prisons have been established in Orasje, Busovaca and Gabela pursuant to appropriate decisions. The decree on district military courts in the territory of HZ-HB during the time of imminent threat of war that was adopted on the 17th of October, 1992, by the Presidency of the HZ-HB, marks the setting of the foundations -- legal foundations for the creation of district prisons in the territory of HZ-HB. In Chapter 6 of this decree, the enforcement of criminal sanctions, the provisions contained in Articles 30 through 35, it is stipulated, for instance in Article 31, and I quote: "Convicted persons shall be sent to serve their prison sentences by the district military courts to the nearest district prison or penitentiary and correctional facility." Since the Gabela prison was -- or, rather, the report of the Department for Judiciary and Administration describes how the Gabela Prison was turned into a detention centre, and I quote: "Because of the war operations and for reasons that had to do with other purposes of these facilities, they were anything but institutions where persons remanded in custody and convicts can be placed." Through arbitrary acts and decisions of bodies that were not competent to make such decisions, they were turned into detention centre without any agreement or monitoring of the superior authorities. That is, again, the same document that I quoted above, Prosecution Exhibit P09551, the work report. At the session of July 19th, 1993, the HVO HZ HB, that's Exhibit P03560, put on the agenda the demand to relocate the persons remanded in custody and isolated persons. That is done at the intervention of the Capljina HVO, and this is listed under miscellaneous, item 7, which means that this was not an item on the agenda that had been prepared in advance. A group was set up, as indicated in the conclusion from this session, in order to improve the conditions of their accommodation and to resolve the situation, the newly-emerged situation. In other words, it was necessary to see what was going on. The first conclusion from this session of the HVO HZ HB, already presented to this Chamber, calls for consistent compliance with the Geneva Conventions, quoting obligations from the decree on the treatment of persons taken prisoner in combat or in armed conflict, which was passed one year before by the HZ-HB Presidency. The real willingness to do so by the provisional body of the executive government is reflected in this conclusion, which reads as follows: I quote: "Access shall be granted to the International Red Cross and other international organisations in order to control the conditions for their accommodation in the facilities where detained persons are located." This position reflects the actual state of mind of the provisional body of the executive government because this is an internal document, the minutes from a meeting, not a propaganda-type document meant for the public at large. At that time, in the second half of July 1993, I wrote a public letter to Mate Granic, the deputy prime minister of the Republic of Croatia - that's document P 3673 - and also four days earlier, that's document 1D 01870. This letter had to do primarily with the implementation of the Makarska Agreement. In this letter, the provisional body of the executive government for the first time makes it public and faces this problem, expressing its readiness to assist in resolving this problem that really did exist, although the provisional body of the executive government, as indicated by all the documents and all the minutes, did not have either de jure or de facto powers over those centres, and that goes also for the conduct of the people there. In this press release, an effort is made to establish some principles that were defined by the provisional organ or provisional body as the, I quote, "unconditional exchange on the all-for-all principle." As I've already pointed out, the HVO HZ-HB took the position that, I quote: "It should be possible to allow access to interested humanitarian organisations to all the facilities where isolated persons who are placed in isolation are housed," which shows that they were obviously willing to resolve this problem as soon as possible and not to hide anything. This press release clearly shows that a call for some actions is made, and through the involvement of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Croatia and international organisations, there is this will to create conditions to really solve this problem. At the same time, these conclusions show that the provisional body of executive government does not manage or run those facilities, and there are no documents where it is possible to find any indication that any decisions could be made, least of all decisions that had to do with the detention issues. We did not have the right to make such operational decisions, and there are no such decisions in the documents at our disposal. The only thing that could be done was to call -- that's the document that I've already referenced, that P 03673, and I quote: "HVO HZ-HB calls on all the bodies to consistently comply with international conventions, both in their treatment of civilians and of prisoners of war." The tone of the press release and the call to set up yet another meeting with the representatives of the government in Sarajevo, in the context of the Makarska Agreement that had been signed some ten days earlier testifies to our efforts to take every measure at our disposal, the comprehensive measures that envisaged all forms of fighting, all forms of crime that were already mentioned in the minutes from the meeting of the 11th and the 18th of August. That's documents P 04111 and 1D 01675, include the following, and I quote: "The Defence and Interior Affairs Departments should see whether it is necessary to establish a mixed unit that would contain personnel from military and civilian police in the town of Mostar in order to provide efficient protection to the citizens against various groups and individuals. And it is in particular necessary to link up and to place under full control various groups that are outside of full command control." At the second meeting on the 18th of August, conclusions are made related to the service of sentences for persons who have already been convicted and whose convictions were final, and who could only be placed in the prisons which were part of the judicial system. In document P 4756, quotes were made from the meeting of the collegium of the Defence Department before this Trial Chamber which clearly show that there is no system because it is quite obvious that nobody knows who was in charge of most of those centres, and this is the information that was at the disposal of the HVO HZ-HB because Bruno Stojic stressed that quite clearly on several occasions at our meetings. The Defence Department was not in charge, but as documents indicate, regardless of this fact, it did take a number of measures to improve the situation. The positions taken at the working meeting of the government of the Croatian Republic on the 6th of September, that's document P 4841, show the commitment to take measures, although it is quite clearly stated in the minutes, and this was our position at the time, unanimous position, that the provisional body of executive government is not responsible for this situation in any way. Defence witnesses will talk about the joint declaration by the president of the Republic of Croatia, Franjo Tudjman, and the president of the BiH Presidency, Alija Izetbegovic, signed in Geneva on the 14th of September, 1993. That's Exhibit P 5051, appointing their special plenary potentiaries for the implementation of those measures, the Foreign Minister Mate Granic and Foreign Minister Haris Silajdzic. Together with the working groups that had been established, they took a number of measures to close down the detention centres and to improve the overall humanitarian situation. I spoke about the necessity of implementing those demands in a lengthy TV programme aired on the 21st of September, 1993, calling on all the bodies to prevent all the conduct that is contrary to Geneva Conventions. That's document 1D 2230. At one of the meetings that I attended, and that was attended by both envoys, Granic and Silajdzic, I demanded that all the conditions on the declaration be met, that all the detention centres be dissolved, threatening, as recorded in the minutes, that I would otherwise be abandoning everything, my position in the government, and that I would be tendering my resignation from all the positions I was holding at the time. The provisional organ of executive government, or the Government itself, had no power to do this on their own, and the document is 1D 01291. Finally, as the Chamber knows, Mate Boban adopted the decision on the 10th of December, 1993, on the unilateral and unconditional dismantling of all detention centres, which eventually led to their closure. I'm trying to keep my presentation as short as possible, but I hope the Chamber will allow me to say a couple of words on the establishment of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. It was established in keeping with the constitutional agreement on the establishment of the union of the republics of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which in itself was envisaged in the international peace package. Throughout the latter half of 1993, there were continuing negotiations about the borders of the republics within the union. The establishment of the Croatian Republic and the establishment of clearer relations for the first time according to the principle of the division of power into the legislative, executive and judicial branches, allowed me to function in a much more professional manner. It took us no more than a month or two to get most of the system up and running, including the financial system. Another thing that I wish to point out is that the relations that were established within the insufficiently defined community, which is what it was prior to this, had not been successful in guaranteeing a more effective functioning in terms of the work of the municipalities and the coordination between municipalities, which was one reason why the breakdown of various responsibilities was never that clear. Early in 1994, we took charge of financing the entire military system, the police, and the health system. Early in 1994, the first pensions were eventually paid to the citizens of Herceg-Bosna, not just to all of its citizens under the control of the HVO. I'm referring to HVO-controlled territory, of course. Rather, there were various forms of compensation, a total of 130.000 from the budget that were paid to Croats in other territories, as well, which is something that the Prosecutor quotes, as well, bases on one of my discussions in the presidential transcripts. This is 27048. That is the transcript reference for this trial. I am quoted as saying that each and every one of the Croats were eventually paid. This was said in a bit to illustrate the difficulty that we were facing in sustaining our budget. Now that I've made a reference to the presidential transcripts, I want to add something about the 5th December meeting in Split where the serious situation that we were facing was discussed. I turned down a proposal by Mate Boban [Realtime translation read in error, "Granic"] on how the government was to be put together, and I added as follows: "I mean, I can't be made to answer for this situation. Why am I being called to account? I am responsible as a member of the Government, but I'm not answering for anything in particular. It is be the minister who should be answerable to the parliament."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The transcript should say "Mate Boban," not "Mate Granic," if we were listening correctly. It's line 21 on page 8. THE ACCUSED PRLIC: Exactly, it was Mate Boban. [Interpretation] This is P 6454, and that's where you can find the relevant quote. After that, I was involved in proposing a setup for the new government. Although it was a mixed composition in terms of personnel, it was capable of carrying out its work in an effective manner. In order to illustrate the objectives of the HR-HB, in my opening speech as the prime-minister of the HR-HB government, at the meeting of the House of Representatives on 20th November 1993, when we were elected, talking for the first time about the programme for 1994, I pointed out the following. I quote: "The fundamental objective of the HR-HB government is to stop the war and stop the ongoing clashes, as well as to create a republic for the Croatian people in which all the other peoples of the BH, the Muslims and the Serbs, and all ethnic minorities will enjoy all human and ethnic rights, in keeping with European standards." At the same time, we are under an obligation to make sure that all Croats in all other areas throughout B and H will be able to enjoy the same rights. If I may make a suggestion to the Chamber, to look at my presentation before the House of Representatives, the presidents of the municipalities of Herceg-Bosna, and the deputies elected to the Council of Municipalities and Council of Citizens of the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina, in May 1994. This is something that was broadcast over the radio, and here I tried to provide an overall picture of the government's work, but also of the provisional organ of executive government prior to that. If the Chamber looks at that, I think you will see the greater picture, the context of what was happening at the time, but it will also be better able to judge my motivation as well as that of others who were involved in the work of other executive bodies of Herceg-Bosna. The results that we managed to achieve will also become clearer, and assessments of some events might then be made that, to some extent, are part of this trial. The document number is 1D 2719. Your Honours, I am now moving on to my second-to-last subject. This is my interview with the OTP. Although to some extent I've been referring to elements of this interview - this is P 9078 - please allow me to shed more light on some of these statements that I made. My interview with the OTP took place in 2001, when the alliance for a change was set up in Bosnia-Herzegovina, which then formed the government, and then for the first time the HDZ was no longer represented in any of the levels of power above county level. Back in 2000, I had left the HDZ, which drew a lot of attention from the media. There were also a number of newspaper articles which had been specially commissioned, of course, to expose and denounce me as a person and to pin on me the responsibility for everything that had been going on during the war, including alleged war crimes. That, however, was not sufficient, so elements of white collar and other kinds of crime were also fabricated, and this kept the newspapers busy for some time, or at least some of them. Of course, I know or can guess who was behind this campaign to discredit me. In addition to all of this, I was labelled as a traitor of the Croatian people. All these attacks were aimed at my person, despite my more or less natural sangfroid, I understood that this was part of the process that all new democracies had to face. Despite all of this, as I say, this gave rise to a certain amount of bitterness, which I then vented in my interview with the OTP. It is true that the OTP served on me a series of questions that they said they would be interested in. There were a total of 24 subjects included. I drafted a special written analysis in relation to each and every one of those areas, and I was prepared to answer all of the questions. However, I succeeded only to a limited extent. I can offer you my views as to why that was the case. First of all, I'd received at a later date a tape-recording of the OTP's interview with Mr. Kresimir Zubak who at the time was the vice president of the provisional organ of executive government. I was then given a chance to cross-reference these and compare his interview to my own. The interview with Mr. Zubak unfolded over five days, and my interview only took two days. It was obvious to me that Mr. Zubak was given sufficient time to address all the same issues that I spoke about, except he was given more time so he could provide more precise and more detailed elucidations. The other thing that I noticed at the time was that the chemistry or the overall atmosphere in those two interviews were entirely different. During my interview, especially if you listened to the actual tape-recording rather than to just read the transcript, there was a certain amount of tension that was in the air, and that was clearly noticeable. I believe that there were several reasons behind this sort of atmosphere. Above all, as you can tell by inspecting the English version, I had to make several corrections to the work of the interpreter, who was using erroneous terminology in relation to a number of truly crucial matters. I wasn't able to catch all the mistakes and all of the omissions, simply because I was trying to focus on the questions and to answer them in the appropriate context. That was the reason that we asked the OTP to put together for us a transcript in Croatian. For example, page 18, there is something missing in the translation. Yugoslav dinars were coming from Croatia following the introduction of the Croatian currency. The wording used by the Prosecutor is missing the adjective "Yugoslav," which lends the entire context a whole new meaning. I believe the other reason to have been the following: The OTP, people come from an entirely different legal background. I think, then as now, it might have been difficult for them to understand the differences between the two systems. I did my best to explain our legal system and my position within that system, the system that applied at the time throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina. As you can see, this led to misunderstanding, and this sidetracked the entire interview. I observed the negative reactions of my interviewers; for example, when I said I simply didn't have the power that my position seems to entitle me to. My impression at the time was that instead of having a conversation, instead of providing explanations, I was merely expected to provide yes-or-no answers to any of their questions. Having heard Mr. Tomjanovic's arguments, and he was one of the persons who spoke to me at the time, who conducted an analysis that the Chamber is aware of, which shows that in actual fact I was never offered a chance, during that interview, to offer not an alternative interpretation but, rather, an authentic interpretation of the laws. I decided to draft a written answer to his own analysis. I have been preparing this reply for quite some time. Since we opted for this opening statement or introduction only as late as ten days ago, which by the way turned my entire provisional release to spending endless hours before my PC, working on my presentation, and I thank the Chamber for granting my provisional release, I have simply not had sufficient time to draw up this reply. However, as an addendum to my presentation, I will be submitting to the Chamber the full and final version of my reply to Tomjanovic's paper. This I will do in a bit to furnish the Chamber with complete and thorough information, thereby enabling the Chamber to make better informed conclusions. When I read the interview now, it is quite clear that the answers in the interview are in some ways incomplete or not sufficiently clear. Some of them demand further clarification. Besides, I have since received a lot of documents that I had not inspected before. Therefore, some of my assessments would now be somewhat different. Above all, I'm referring to the 27th of December, 1991, conversation. This is P 89. I first set eyes on it when it was published in Professor Ribicic's book. He testified as an expert witness before this Tribunal and also brought along the transcript itself. I read the transcript for the first time. It is full of hypothetical statements and assumptions. In addition to this, I had not been able to inspect a number of documents that now became available. The conclusion that I reached was more or less the same as that reached by Professor Ribicic. I simply disregarded the context in which the conversation took place. The message was clear: Pursue negotiations and try to avoid war, and this message was put across by those who called on the Croatian people two months later to vote for Bosnia-Herzegovina's independence at a referendum. That is why I stated in the interview that there was another political possibility that was being held in reserve, just in case. There was a secondary political objective under consideration, to have part of the territory join the Republic of Croatia, should Bosnia and Herzegovina break up. At first I was quite impressed by the transcript, but there is something that I wish to say to the Chamber: you have the minutes of the provisional organ of executive government and the government of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. Those are over 100 sets of minutes, none of which make a single reference to any division of Bosnia and Herzegovina, nor was there any such reference made in what was not included in the minutes, nor was it ever mentioned at those sessions. We will call witnesses who will speak about that, and you do have minutes. They have been admitted into evidence. Again at page 16, I say that I was not in a position to talk about the intentions of the people who had created Herceg-Bosna, because at that time I did not know them at all. I took my positions after having read those documents for the first time, or almost a year after they were adopted, and I could get a full picture only after I was given access to the full set of documents of the HDZ dated 1991, which I mentioned yesterday. In my interview, I tried to depict the relations as they really existed, but I also tried to describe how those organs had been set up de jure in a community that really had a structure that was sui generis. At page 33 of the interview, especially if a person who does not have any previous knowledge reads it, the explanation of my role looks insufficiently articulated. As I explained yesterday, the passing of the statutory decision about the executive government and the character of my appointment, this was signed by Mate Boban, as the president of the HVO. It was very clearly determined, as I was told at the beginning, "You have nothing to do with the military and the police, you have nothing to do with the passing of the Rules of Procedure." This indicates what my position was as the member of -- as a member of this collective body. Those are facts. Outside of the sessions, outside of the conclusions reached at those sessions, I did not have any discretionary powers to take any independent decisions about anything. That was the position in all the executive bodies in our system. That is why I said, at page 36, that in essence I was not the president of the HVO. I explained that yesterday, in part, by describing the evolution of this body from the spring to the summer of 1992, and in particular through the amendments of the relevant documents such as, for instance, the Decree on the Armed Forces from October 1992. That is why I used the abbreviation "PIO." This means the Provisional Executive Body, both in the interview and in my presentation here in court. To cut the long story short, there were three HVOs; the military, that was again the term used for the executive bodies in the municipalities, and the same term again was used for the provisional organ of executive government. This all stems from history, from the past, from the anti-fascist struggle. That was when the boards for national liberation were set up, and that was the term that was used for all the bodies at all the levels. I have already explained that the powers of the HVO HZ-HB were reduced after the amendments were passed on the 14th of August, 1992, which was the time when Mate Boban ceased to be the head of this body. This explains my views at page 47 of the interview where I say that I really did not have any function, because I could not make any decisions either formally, or actually, without going to the collective organ. My resentments [Realtime transcript read in error "reassessment"] at the events that were going on around me at the time of the interview were expressed, among other things, when I said that I had been used by some people, at the time when I was needed to help set up a functioning economic system. This is what I said at page 49, and this is what I said in the letter that I wrote when I left the HDZ ranks, saying that I had never actually been with those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: One correction, because it's rather point at this point in time, Your Honours. Where it says "my resentment," and that would be, I believe, on line 20, page 18, it's "my bitterness." Page 16, I'm sorry. Page 16, not 20, it's "my bitterness," not "resentment." Or not "reassessment," but "my bitterness." THE ACCUSED PRLIC: [Interpretation] Our views were different, but that is business as usual in other parties. But given the circumstances and the fact that emotions ran high, this is a characteristic of that time and of the people from our region. Some people, including myself, may have said some things we shouldn't have said. Some people were against me. I mentioned some of them, because I believe that they were against me. That’s how it was, and there was nothing more to it. The part of the interview at page 55 looks quite confusing, partly because the consecutive interpretation failed to render everything that was actually said. This is where I say something that I've already mentioned; that no information from the security services ever reached me, which is quite obvious from the documents that have been admitted into evidence in this case, because all those reports contained the list of addressees. The debates that we had at the sessions, they are mentioned in the minutes, including the intervention by Bruno Stojic about the current situation. Yesterday, I briefly spoke about the decisions on the internal organisation of the Defence Department, which quite clearly and explicitly stipulate that the military and the civilian segments should be separate. The Defence Department, let me stress once again, primarily had a civilian function, and that is how it acted at the sessions of the provisional organ of executive government, which I say when I stress that the military part of the defence was separate and was operating independently from the provisional organ of the executive government. The provisional organ of executive government, in this case as in other cases, merely appointed the assistance to the heads at the recommendation of the head, himself. This is a technical issue. The experience and the practice of the former Yugoslav system, including the republics, was such that the executive councils never had anything to do with the military and never had anything to do with the security services. The services and the military were responsible to the presidencies or the presidents of the state or of the republics or the political parties and the assemblies. And Herceg-Bosna was no exception; nothing changed there. When I spoke about what Bruno Stojic had said at those meetings, I would like to say that those were not military reports. I stress that at page 94. For the most part, they had to do with problems related to the non-functioning of the system, particularly as it related to mobilisation or funding. We did not have any military information. This had indeed not been envisaged anywhere. The people in the military were under no obligation to do that. They had their commander-in-chief, so that I did not have any right to make any complaints to the commander-in-chief in this regard, as indicated at page 96 of the interview. I did know Petkovic and Praljak, but I was under no obligation to provide any official information to them, and they, in turn, were under no obligation to provide any official information to me. Our contacts were sporadic and quite accidental, except at two or three meetings that were attended by the members of the provisional executive body. As for Valentin Coric, I met with him even more seldom. Of course, that was up until the establishment of the government of the Croatian republic of Herceg-Bosna whose member he was. As far as I can recall, we're talking about one or two meetings of the coordination of the body for fighting crime, which was set up pursuant to the action plan for the fight against crime that was put together as the sessions of the 11th and the 18th of August, 1993. I've already made references to that. In accordance with the topics for the discussion that I had received from the Prosecution, I tried to present the basics of the judiciary in this interview, and I was only partially successful in this effort. But the Trial Chamber has at its disposal all the relevant decrees, you're all lawyers, and you can see the relationship between the prosecutor's offices, prisons, courts, that are the same as in all other countries with the civil law system. At page 88 of the interview, there is some discussion about the Gabela Prison. Pursuant to -- this prison was set up pursuant to Article 145, paragraph 2, of the Law on the Enforcement of Criminal and Misdemeanour Sanctions of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and according to the reports of the judiciary department, it was part of the network that comprised four district, military and civilian prisons in Herceg-Bosna, prisons that were quite logically linked to the relevant courts, courts that had jurisdiction in those areas. But as I've already noted, the same reports state that in the second half of 1993, neither the courts nor the judiciary department had any access to some of the places that were used to detain prisoners. Moreover, some facilities that were set up as prisons were turned into detention centres without any decisions having been passed by the relevant higher organs. Enough documents have already been admitted into evidence and are at the disposal of Your Honours about how this facility functioned, who the reports went to, and who -- whom it was responsible to. I've already mentioned at page 87 that barracks were used to house detainees. They are mentioned even earlier in 1992 as facilities where detainees were kept. This was -- this is obvious from the agreements that were signed in Geneva under the auspices of the ICRC, where mention is made of the prison in Dretelj. I was able to learn that in that year, it was actually run by HOS, and the Capljina prison. Finally, let me say that in several places in my interview, for instance, at page 82, I spoke about the perpetrators of the crimes that occur in every war. I said that they were committed mostly by people wearing uniforms, by soldiers, members of the military units, military conscripts, and that these people should be punished, regardless of who they are. And I'm absolutely sure that none of the accused here is opposed to that. Quite the contrary. Let me make a brief summary at the end, Your Honours, in light of my alleged contribution to the alleged joint criminal enterprise, presented by the Prosecution in several subparagraphs, in paragraph 17(1). I will refer to the same subparagraphs using the same letters. A, so this is in answer to the allegations contained in the indictment. A: It has already been noted that the HVO HZ-HB was not the highest body in the defence system, that was the HVO as a military organisation, as the military. My role in the provisional organ of executive government did not cover any military affairs, either de facto or de jure, as has already been shown. Enough has been said about the decisions that were issued in accordance with the Rules of Procedure. Your Honours, there is not a single decision passed in accordance with the Rules Of Procedure that would be discriminatory and that would allow the alleged objectives of the joint criminal enterprise to be implemented. B. The goals of the policies were established in the platforms of the HDZ of BH and peace plans, in no uncertain terms. None of those documents contain any indications about the alleged goals of the joint criminal enterprise. At that time, I was not a member of the HDZ. C. My role in the provisional organ of executive government, as a collective organ, has shown -- was shown to be such that any alleged influence over the work of the departments, including the three departments singled out by the Prosecutor, is patently unfounded. D. I stand behind all the -- or stand by all the decisions of the collective body that I signed. None of those decisions could be taken to support the alleged goals of the joint criminal enterprise, including the ones that were singled out in particular by the Prosecution. Let me address two of them now. The decree on the use of abandoned housing, P 3809, was meant to coordinate the work of various municipalities, because they had already passed such decisions. It made it possible to allocate housing apartments on a temporary basis, up to one year, but any apartments that had been abandoned under duress could not be disposed of. HVO HZB did not allocate any apartments, any such apartments to anybody. On the other hand, the Sarajevo government made it possible to allocate apartments on a permanent basis, which was one of the greatest problems in the implementation of the Dayton Peace Agreement. As members of the council of ministers of Bosnia-Herzegovina with the support of the International Community, we decided that everybody had the right to go back to their own apartment, even though those apartments were actually socially owned, which, for instance, is not the case in the Republic of Croatia. The Republic of Croatia never adopted such a decree. The decree on border crossings at state borders simply applied a previous federal regulation that had already been adopted by B and H, defining the state border with the Republic of Croatia, whereas the indictment claims that the aim was to have Herceg-Bosna annexed by the Republic of Croatia. This is P 1560. Item E. The decision we took was exactly the opposite from trying to monitor all the municipalities. We took a decision to have democratically-elected assemblies in each and every of the municipalities where it was possible. The municipalities were fundamental agents of government, and their presidents were members of the legislative body, the Presidency, and later also of the House of Delegates of the HR-HB who appointed members of the HVO, and all the members, including me, answered to them and submitted reports to them. The Prosecutor refers to a decision taken by Mostar Municipality on refugees. I had never previously heard of this before I was interviewed. We have documents available to us, and we will be tendering those, showing that the municipalities took dozens of decisions that were patently contrary to some of the laws passed by the provisional organ of executive government. Appointments throughout municipalities were of a technical nature precisely because the bodies in charge throughout the municipalities made the relevant proposals. The decisions, for the most part, were signed by the president of the HZ-HB. It was in no more than a handful of cases that the decisions were signed by the HVO HZ-HB. For example, as the Prosecutor points out, Ljubuski is a case in hand. The president of the HVO was Milan Simic, who was legitimately elected mayor in the democratic elections that were held in 1990. F. The Prosecutor allegations that there was such a thing as Croatisation [as interpreted], which is a term that occurs in none of the world's dictionaries, Your Honours. It is simply a word that does not exist. They back this by showing decrees in relation to the establishment of the university and institutions of primary/secondary education, the Croatian dinar as a currency used for cash transactions, but also the use of the Croatian coat of arms on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina that was at the time at least half a century old. Defence evidence will demonstrate that these decrees were adopted because of the need to bring life back to normal in areas in which the republican bodies had ceased to function after the war had escalated, and these decrees never discriminated against anyone. G. Contrary to the allegations made by the OTP about the measures -- the financial measures that were adopted, and the system of payments that was established with full recognition for the sovereignty of Bosnia-Herzegovina, this probably represented the single-most important contribution to its economic recovery, bearing in mind the many people from Bosnia-Herzegovina who lived abroad, who were continually contributing to the joint defence of Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina and were, in fact, contributing funds by sending funds to a single account which the Chamber is aware of. It still remains unknown, especially after we've heard testimony about how much money had actually arrived from Croatia during the war, whether Croatia, in fact, backed Herceg-Bosna in its defence at all, all the more so bearing in mind the vested interests of Croatia to help mount a defence in order to preserve its own territory from the same aggressor. Instances of assistance to the Muslim people in government in Sarajevo by Croatia, they have been documented throughout this trial and will continue to be documented, both as it concerned putting up refugees, treatment in Croatian hospitals, education, organising and delivering humanitarian aid, supplying weapons, and training entire units of the BH Army. H. The non-existence of a provisional executive body in military matters, this is something that has been inspected quite closely. Preparations for defence plans were, as I pointed out before, only about the civilian aspect of defence in schools, banks, kindergartens, and other such institutions. This is illustrated by 1D 2722, 1D 2723, 1D 2724, and 1D 2811. I. As a member of the provisional executive body, I was in no position to appoint or, indeed, replace or dismiss anyone on my own. Mine was a single vote, and the same applied to everyone else. Normally, this vote, was used to back proposals that were made, proposals that had already been endorsed by the one of the winning parties or a candidate's municipality. J. The decision on military production was a decision that had to do with the economy primarily - it was in relation to both ABiH and HVO - while the decree of the Republic of B and H, the envisaged production only for one of the components of the armed forces, the BH Army. K. The cooperation with Croatia in its various aspects is purportedly seen as a crime. An example cited is the adoption of the decision on the import of goods from Croatia. I explained yesterday that this was a reciprocal measure because goods from the BiH were handled the same way when being imported to Croatia. EU countries, NAFTA in North America, and all the countries throughout the region enjoy free trade with no restrictions. In the present case, however, the Prosecutor seems to believe that a measure like that constituted a war crime. L. The decision taken on the 15th of January, 1993, did not in any way affect the commencement of clashes. It was adopted and withdrawn pursuant to orders and information supplied by the head of the Croatian negotiating team, the president of the HDZ and HZ HB, Mate Boban This was done in good faith and with a view to setting up a joint command. Dozens of agreements had been signed to that effect. Another objective was to avoid clashes between the two parties, and now I'm giving you a definition of the entire conflict under consideration here. It is a conflict that can be considered an internal conflict between two components of a single armed force on part of the free territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That's my definition, and I'm saying that as the defence minister who prepared the first law on the armed forces of the federation when these formations were formally merged. The period that followed the 15th of January is the only period in which the HVO HZ-HB emerged as one of the addressees when information was submitted on the situation that was unfolding in Gornji Vakuf, where clashes had already erupted prior to the 15th of January, as we have all witnessed. M. In April 1993, again, there was no ultimatum whatsoever. Both parties had already signed the Vance-Owen Plan by this time, and we're talking about its implementation. Defence evidence will show that clashes in parts of the territory had nothing whatsoever to do with the HVO HZ-HB meeting that was held on the 3rd of April, a meeting devoted in its entirety to documents related to the Vance-Owen Plan and preparations for its exceptionally complex implementation, which in effect meant the dissolution of Herzeg-Bosna. N. The provisional organ of executive government never opened nor exercised any control over any of the detention centres referenced in the indictment. The HVO HZ-HB, in order to restore order, activated, based on republican regulations and the legislation of the Presidency of the HZ-HB, institutions of the judiciary, civilian and military, the prosecution offices, as well as courts, prisons, in which, under the law, prisoners could only be kept pursuant to a decision from an appropriate court. O. There is no evidence at all showing that the HVO HZ-HB was in any way involved in anything to do with forced labour performed by detainees. P. The provisional executive body did not take a single decision, and you have all the minutes, you have all the copies of the Official Gazette, that discriminated against the Muslim population, or anyone else, for that matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Defence will lead evidence to get the Chamber a full picture regarding the functioning of the Office for Refugees, which was an institution with a humanitarian remit. They offered all possible assistance to persons whose lives were at risk, especially refugees, regardless of their ethnicity, and it was certainly not involved in any deportations. There is nothing to corroborate the alleged activities by the Commission for Population Migrations, something else that is referenced by the Prosecutor in the Indictment. R. It is malicious to suggest that this assistance in receiving over 100.000 Croat refugees, because of military action by the BH Army; for example, in Zenica, Travnik, Kakanj, Konic [phoen], Bugojno, Fojnica or Vares, was aimed at getting the Croats to leave the areas in which they were residing. This was not the case, and this is in fact demonstrated by the fact that most of them left for Croatia, while very few actually remained under relatively difficult conditions in Herceg-Bosna, but certainly not in Mostar. S. Reactions to attacks by the Muslim army against Croats, which was something that led to tens of thousands of citizens being displaced, cannot be considered as an attempt to spread fear, hatred, and distrust. Croats were, in fact, expelled from territories historically inhabited by Croats, and this is something that the Prosecutor places under quotation marks, because their ancestors had been living in those areas for at least a thousand years previously. Mostar was defined as the capital of the province and then also the capital of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, as well as of the Herzegovinian Neretva County in the Federation. Proposals were even made for Mostar to become the capital of the entire Federation, and the Muslim negotiators agreed with this. The 30th of June declaration, of which I spoke yesterday, is a mere declaration. It is certainly not an order or a decision. T. All the humanitarian convoys that ever travelled through HZ-HB territory reached their destination. The protocol that was defined in cooperation with international organisations helped to work out a procedure for this. In addition to this, the Defence will be showing that no request by international organisations to furnish humanitarian aid was ever refused, regardless of its eventual destination. U. As has already been pointed out, the provisional executive organ had no role to play in any of the military operations. Contrary to allegations made by the OTP, it was a reconstruction of whatever had been destroyed, including the cultural and historic heritage of all of the ethnic groups, was one of its primary commitments. I am quoting the following documents: 1D 02703, 1D 02706. V. The body that I was a member of, as is suggested by the Prosecution in its contradictory allegation, through the establishment of the bodies of the internal affairs and judicial bodies created conditions for the crimes to be prosecuted. The Defence will show, through its document and witnesses, that the fight against crime was a continuous effort and that the HVO HZ-HB and the government of the HR-HB, later on, involved all the competent institutions in those activities. Operation Pauk, Spider, had as its task the criminal prosecution of all the crimes that documents existed for, in particular major ones, including war crimes. After that, I participated in building the judicial bodies of the BH Federation. We entrusted those tasks to them. After the signing of the Dayton Agreement, as I said yesterday, an agreement was signed on special conditions for the criminal prosecution of the war crimes in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the so-called Rome rules of the road, that stipulated that nobody could be indicted for war crimes without the approval of the OTPW. The evidence admitted so far and the testimony of witnesses indicated I was quite clear in my contacts with international representatives, urging them for their support and assistance in resolving the current situation related to the detention of a large number of military conscripts. I had no reason not to tell the truth either then, or now. What I said in public was meant to urge the dissolution of all the detention centres and the release of all prisoners. All the documents without exception say that the provisional body of executive government demanded full compliance with international humanitarian law and unimpeded access to the ICRC. The last letter of the alphabet that I will use is X. For the first time, the Prosecution is partially right when it alleges that I always said that individual crimes were committed by elements that were outside of anyone's control, loose cannons, because I was not aware of any decisions by any official bodies related to this. This is what I believe today. They were not an organised activity mounted by the institutions that had anything to do with the provisional organ of executive government. I condemned all kinds of criminal behaviour, and I relayed the information about investigations that had been conducted, and which, as we heard here, I had received, to the international mediators. Your Honours, so much for my contribution to what I believe is the non-existence -- nonexistent joint criminal enterprise. Let me repeat once again. I sympathise with all the war victims. These are people who lived side by side with me in the same city, people with whom I lived all my life, or with their families. I can say that with the provisional body of executive government and later on with the government, I did all I could, and believe me, really everything I could under those circumstances, to assuage the consequences of the war and the destruction that was caused during the war and to punish those who committed crimes. This is what I thought, this is what I did at the time, in the difficult circumstances, and this is what I still think now, now that I'm able to look at all the documents and all the information that I did not have at my disposal at the time. The developments have shown that we were unable to resolve the problems with the Muslim politicians, but we made every effort to ensure that the Croatian Bosnian Federation actually started functioning after that. I initialed the Dayton Peace Agreement, and after that, for more than five years, I represented Bosnia and Herzegovina as the foreign minister. I represented all its citizens. If you look at my career, you will see that apart from just a few years, I spent all my time in Sarajevo, where I always felt that I was welcomed by all, and this is where I lived at the time when the indictment was served. Thank you very much for your attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We are about to take a 20-minute break, and after the break we will hear the first witness as scheduled so that we can start with the examination-in-chief. We will resume in 20 minutes; that is, at 4.00 sharp. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. I believe Mr. Scott wanted to say something.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, thank you. Mr. President, Your Honours, good afternoon, and good afternoon to all those in and around the courtroom. Your Honour, I wanted to raise two important matters before we continue further. Out of deference to Mr. Prlic, I did not want to either delay or interrupt his statement, but there were two matters I think should be addressed before we continue. First of all, Your Honours, the Prosecution would move for the unsealing and making public of Mr. Prlic's prior statement, which is Exhibit P 09078, which this Trial Chamber, as you know, has previously admitted into evidence. While the litigation concerning the admission of that statement was ongoing, the statement had been placed under seal. However, it appears that notwithstanding the Chamber's decision admitting that statement now, that the statement has remained under seal and not available to the public or anyone else, for that matter. And, Your Honour, the Prosecution does not see any reason at this point why that particular piece of evidence, unlike the other voluminous evidence in this case today should be secret or under seal, especially -- especially in light of the fact that in the last two days, yesterday and today, Mr. Prlic himself has, on numerous occasions, referred both to the existence of the statement and the content of the statement, and in fact has, well, tried to correct or change some of the statements that he made in that statement. I think it's only fair that that statement be a matter of open evidence that anyone can review at this time. So, Your Honour, the Prosecution moves that Exhibit P 09078, the previous statement -- written statement or testimony, a transcript, actually, of Mr. Prlic be unsealed and made a public exhibit, number 1. Number 2, Your Honour, the Prosecution must raise its concerns and objections to the practice so far, only at this early moment in the Defence cases, in connection with the information provided so far concerning Defence witnesses and statements; that is, their evidence. And before Mr. Karnavas gets too excited about that, let me assure him that I intend to make a measured statement and to acknowledge, in fact, some steps that Mr. Karnavas has taken. But, Your Honours, since we are now starting the Defence cases, and as everyone in the courtroom knows, we will be engaged in this process now for some months. It seems to the Prosecution entirely appropriate to raise this at the outset so that we can hopefully, if you will, get off on the right foot. And of course we would expect this to apply to all the Defence cases and not just the Prlic Defence, but the six Defence teams. Indeed, it may be that some of the other Defence teams already intend or contemplate a different practice, and I cannot speak to that except to say that, of course, we're starting with the Prlic Defence case, so that is the case that I must direct at least my immediate comments to. Now, Your Honour, with respect, the Zuzul statement, and if the Chamber has it, and I hope that the Chamber might -- at least one of the Judges might have it at hand. If the Chamber looks at the Zuzul witness statement that was filed as part of the Rule 65 ter G Defence filings, the Prosecution respectfully submits that the summary is deficient and is not what Rule 65 ter(G)(i)(b) requires. What the Prosecution submits must be summarised is not simply the background information on the witness, that is, what positions he or she have held in the past, and must be more than simply even a listing of the topics or subjects on which the witness will testify. What the Rule requires, in our submission, is an actual statement of the substantial -- not every word and of course not a verbatim statement, but a substantial and detailed summary of what the witness's actual evidence will be, not what he -- where he was during the war, not what his positions were during the war, but what his or her evidence will actually be. And if I can remind the Chamber -- excuse me. If I can refer the Chamber to the Rule itself, and I'm quoting now Rule 65 ter (G)(i)(b), it requires, "a summary of the facts," and I underline the word "facts," "a summary of the facts on which each witness will testify." And I invite the Chamber again, if you will turn your attention, please, to the summary for Mr. Zuzul, which is the first witness listed in the Prlic 65 ter (G) witness list. The first paragraph and the first sentence of the second paragraph is entirely information -- which we appreciate but is readily available from any number of sources, is entirely information about various positions he has held. He was deputy foreign minister at one point. He was at the United Nations at one point, et cetera, et cetera. Then the last full one-third of the summary is simply a statement that says, in practical effect: "Having sat through meetings that were recorded and referred to in the presidential transcripts, Mr. Zuzul's testimony will touch upon a significant portion of the alleged JCE." "Will touch upon the JCE." And then the rest of the summary essentially is a paraphrase of paragraph 15 of the Prosecutor's indictment, which with all respect we don't necessarily need to be reminded of, but we appreciate it. But, Your Honour, if you look is the summary in substance, not the number of lines, not the number of words on the page, but if Your Honours, President Antonetti, Judge Trechsel, Judge Prandler, if you will look at the actual words on the page and what's said here, there's almost no information provided to the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you forgot Judge Mindua.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My apologies, Judge. My apologies to that, as well as to you, Judge. If you will look at the summary, and again, my apologies. You will find that -- you will find almost no information, almost no information by which the Prosecution can reasonably prepare to meet the evidence of this witness. We'll talk about the JCE. We'll talk about the JCE. That's about 99 per cent of what it says. Now, beyond that, Your Honour, what compounds the problem in this situation, what compounds the problem, unlike the Prosecution witnesses, we've not received any statement of this witness, no statement of the witness whatsoever, and I don't know if the Chamber has. I assume the Chamber hasn't, or if it was, I would assume the Prosecution would be provided a copy of the same. I see the Chamber shaking its head in a negative response, saying they have not. If that's the case, Your Honour, then both the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution are working at a substantial disadvantage in being able to prepare to receive this witness's testimony, and that simply puts everyone in the courtroom at a substantial disadvantage and was not the practice followed by the Prosecution. The Chamber will know that with the Prosecution witnesses, there was at least always at least one detailed multi-page statement, sometimes multiple statements, sometimes verbatim transcripts of prior testimony, by which the evidence could be reviewed and a cross-examiner could prepare his cross-examination accordingly. I might add that these are not easy witnesses. This is not a criminal case where a witness comes in and says, "I think I saw the suspect run out of the door. I think the suspect was wearing a blue coat." In cross-examination, that witness can be prepared, perhaps, perhaps reasonably easily. We're talking now about cross-examination on a whole host of issues. The only information we have is evidence touching on the JCE, evidence touching on the JCE. Now we've been provided one, two, three, four, five, six, seven binders of documents with no prior statement and no sufficient summary to prepare -- to prepare to meet this evidence, and, Your Honour, that's simply not efficient. Now, I said I wanted to be fair to Mr. Karnavas, because I did raise this with him, and he was kind enough, and I do thank him, yesterday to provide a proofing note, presumably after meeting with Mr. Zuzul over the weekend or at some time, of about a page and a half of a letter, about a page and a half of a letter, which I think the Chamber may have also received. Now, again, let me be measured. I appreciate and I thank Mr. Karnavas for having provided that letter, but it is, in itself, an anomaly and actually illustrates the Prosecution's point. A proofing note is prepared to supplement and to correct, if necessary, a prior statement, so that the person -- the opposing party, the people preparing to meet that evidence, are duly advised, are duly advised of any additions or corrections to the statement, but it is an anomaly, one that we appreciate but nonetheless an anomaly, to get a proofing note that corrects or supplements something that doesn't exist. We have no statement. We have no statement, and all we know is we have seven binders of documents concerning the evidence of a witness which will touch upon the JCE. Now, Your Honour, that's, among other things -- it also represents a matter of fundamental fairness to the process and in relation to the Prosecution witnesses. There cannot, Your Honours, there cannot be a rule or a practice that says that Prosecution witnesses are subject to greater scrutiny and greater testing of their evidence than Defence witnesses. With a Prosecution witness, we must have a prior statement. With a Prosecution witness, we can test any inconsistencies with prior statements. But with the Defence witness, well, we'll give the Defence witness a pass. We'll make it the Defence witness, we don't have to do that. The Defence witness is not subject to the same scrutiny or to have his or her evidence tested to the same degree as a Prosecution witness. That is a double standard that the Trial Chamber should not accept. It is further, Your Honours, a matter of efficiency, and while that word is sometimes given a bad rap, if you will, efficiency is absolutely required if this trial process can move forward at any sort of a pace that the Trial Chamber, I know and we all know, wishes it to proceed. But in order to allow opposing counsel or opposing parties to prepare, there must be adequate information provided. The Chamber knows, according to the Chamber's requirements and guidelines, that the cross-examining party has to provide copies of cross-examination exhibits. They have to be prepared in advance, and, by necessity, even far before the direct examination is finished because you can't make 15 copies of voluminous documents in five minutes. So when the direct examination finishes, we can't just automatically produce all the documents for cross-examination in 15 copies that have been organised and with no previous information having been received about the witness. So, Your Honour, not only is it an issue -- Your Honours, it is not only an issue of fairness. It is also one of efficiency, which touches on fairness, because then what the Prosecution is required to do, and with respect, what the Prosecution has been required to do concerning Mr. Zuzul is make some sort of guess, "Well, it's going to touch upon the JCE," and therefore we have to be over-broad, over-inclusive in the material that we prepare, in the amount of documents that we select, that our trial support staff and others then have to prepare, because we don't know what the actual evidence of the witness who is coming is going to be. Your Honour, in our respectful submission, these raise serious issues. This is not a technical matter. This raises serious issues as to the fundamental fairness of the process, and not only disadvantages the Prosecution, but, frankly, it disadvantages the Judges as well. So, Your Honour, we would ask the Chamber to address this matter and that full and fair -- at least full and fair summaries be provided. And in addition, if at all possible, statements for the witness can be provided. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may be heard --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Before hearing you, and of course we will hear you with great interest, but I would like to ask Mr. Scott whether he has some proposal or motion regarding the hearing of this witness today, tomorrow, and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I do. I think that in this particular instance, hoping that we can adopt a different procedure in the future, but we can't today, we can't now with a fact, if you will, with respect, our proposal would be that assuming that we can complete the -- assuming that the direct examination of this witness and any further of the other Defence questioning that we've discussed by the other Defence teams, assuming that all that questioning can be completed by Thursday, that now having received for the first time to know what the evidence is that the Prosecution is required to meet, we think that if that is the case, and since and only, and only because Monday is a holiday and only because our team is willing to work through the weekend, that if we -- if the evidence -- other evidence is completed by Thursday, we would be prepared to begin cross-examination on Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. Excuse me, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's okay, Your Honour. Let me address that last point because I think it's false for the Prosecution to stand here and say, with a straight face, that this is the first time they know of the evidence, and I think it would be false for the Judges to look me in the eye and say that is the case, as well, because as of March 31st, you, Your Honours, as well as the Prosecutor, were provided, as well as my colleagues, with the number of documents that this witness, along with the other witnesses, would talk about. So he had ample time to look through. He's had years to read those documents. Many of the documents are "P" documents. "P" stands for what? "Prosecution." "D" documents stand for "Defence," some of which are already entered into evidence, others of which are connected to the "P" Prosecution documents. Therefore, I find it rather ironic - in fact it's supremely ironic - for of all people, Mr. Scott, who knows this case better than anybody, working seven, eight years on it, to sit here and say that now, for the first time, he's dumbfounded and now he's going to have to need time to prepare to challenge the JCE of which Mr. Zuzul will touch upon. That's number 1. Number 2, the Rules do not require for me to take statements. That is very, very clear. We only need to provide summaries. Third, may I point out, may I point out that on March 31st, we provided the summaries as we were required. As of March 31st, Your Honours as well as the Prosecutor had those summaries. As of March 31st, the Prosecutor could have -- could have raised that issue, as opposed to today. And I won't go into any reasons why today he chose to spend 20 minutes addressing this issue, but he could have raised it. We even had a hearing, and I believe that was on the 21st. It wasn't raised back then. So clearly, if Mr. Scott had a problem with the summaries, I think acting due diligently, especially when he indicated that he is overly concerned about -- I believe the word "efficiency" was used, then he should have brought it well in advance when we could have addressed it on the 21st. And, of course, had I been ordered to provide additional information, I probably would have been able to do so under the circumstances. Now, the Rules do not say that I have to do a statement or that I have to go through each and every document and pointing out exactly what part of the document I'm going to refer to. For instance, we have presidential transcripts. In those presidential transcripts, many of which we have seen here, some of them have Mr. Zuzul in. Now, you don't have to be a 25-year veteran, a career prosecutor, to figure out that you're going to be focusing, among other things, on what Mr. Zuzul said, or at least knowing based on the little tidbit I gave him, because he's claiming that I've been, you know, rather stingy with my parceling of my information to him, that probably I would be asking Mr. Zuzul, since he was present during those discussions, to give us some insight, and I believe I might have even used that word once or twice, maybe even in my proofing notes, that he would give insight. So I don't see where the problem lies. If you look at other documents. For instance, we have the Friendship And Cooperation Agreement. How often have we seen that document? How many witnesses were paraded by the Prosecution? So is there something in that document that I can possibly yank out that isn't there on the four corners of the page? Of course not. But if you look at my summary, you'll see that Mr. Zuzul was an active participant, you know, almost shadowing in some ways Mr. Tudjman on events, and so he has some insight. You know, the JCE talks about the carving up of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That's going to be one of the issues, okay? Maybe he'll talk about the confederation issue because that's touched upon. So if you glean through the documents, Your Honours, it's -- you don't have to be a veteran. In fact, with no disrespect to Stevie Wonder, even he could see exactly where I'm going if he had these documents. It's that plain and simple. Now, that said, Mr. Scott contacted me. We have been rather busy primarily because of the last-minute circumstances. I understand that he had some concerns. I tried to address them as best as I could. I made a phone call. I spoke with the case manager, and as he well knows and as I well know, that sometimes, you know, it's a lot more difficult to get -- even once the witness is here, to sit down and actually get all the information in an appropriate time to get it to the other party. I finished the proofing notes - although Mr. Scott doesn't like the fact that I characterized them as proofing notes, but in fact that's what they were - Sunday night at approximately 12.00 or 1.00, and one of my staff, who actually was still working Sunday night. Unfortunately, we weren't able to e-mail it until the morning probably because we were still trying to deal with other technical issues. I take Mr. Scott to heart. I will sit down with him. I will ask him concretely what more information would he have liked to have seen. I don't agree with what he's saying, that he cannot cross-examine until next week, and frankly I would oppose to that. I would oppose to it vehemently, and I'll tell you why. First, I think we're going to be through with the questioning way before Thursday, but even if it only takes us to Thursday, I would ask that we not handle it next week. Why? Because all the other witnesses are preprogramed. I had his colleague -- Mr. Stringer asked me, "Are we still on for the next witness?" And I said, "Yes." So if now we have to use up Tuesday with Mr. Zuzul, it throws everything off because everybody is preprogramed. I would suggest, and I want to be fair to Mr. Scott -- God knows I would love for him to feel at the end of the case that we on the Defence side have been fair to the Prosecution. I would suggest that we pick a further date down the road, and I would suggest -- we have two particular weeks in mind; one -- because I anticipated Mr. Scott standing up and making a big fuss. He's predictable in some ways, as I am too. We have two weeks in particular. One is the Friday of 18 July. Now, I haven't mentioned this with Mr. Zuzul, but that week we happen to be going five days, and that would not upset the axis, as it were. You know, the other one would be the following Monday, which is Monday, the 21st of July, because we're due to sit all day that day. So I would say that if, and that's a big qualifier, if we run out of time or if the Prosecution needs additional time, then we can choose those two days, and I don't think that they can cry foul because, one, they have more time to prepare. Two, they have -- you know, it's well in advance, they're not going to be prejudiced in any way. And, three, and more importantly, this has happened to us at least on two or three prior occasions. So -- but I would not agree with his assessment that -- or his urging the Trial Chamber to adopt a rule that is not in the Rules, that has been heavily discussed, having sat on the Rules committee myself, you know, that the Defence is not obligated to provide a statement. They're entitled to provide summaries, and of course if the summaries are incomplete, we can provide more, more information. If that's his problem, we can go through the witnesses. I'm willing to sit down. This is the first that I've heard that it was so complicated that they're unable to do their cross-examination, but again I want to emphasise that they've had the documents. In fact, all the binders that they've had, we've streamlined it. We've added one or two, of which we gave notice, but, by and large, all the other documents that they've had, with the exception that some have already been trimmed out because we're trying to be as efficient as possible. And I must say that it is not sometimes until you -- the witness comes to The Hague and you proof them, because some of these witnesses are extremely busy. I don't have the same power of subpoena or the same august presence, as it were, as the Prosecution. When he shows up at the presidential palace, you know, they know he's from the Office of the Prosecution. When I go, I'm like Oliver Twist with a cup in hand, knocking, saying, "Please, would you let me in," you know. So it's not easy for me to get all these witnesses to actually sit down with me in the field for a detailed analysis, you know, but we will do our level best. Finally, let me address the first issue. Of course, we would agree with the Prosecution that the statement should have been made public. After all, the reason that we kept it -- I had moved that it not be public on the grounds that it was still being litigated. And once we had a final conclusion on that, there is no other reason, and I don't see any confidential information in there so obviously we want a public trial. We've stressed it from the very beginning. We have nothing to hide, and so we concur and we join the Prosecution in that motion. See, here is a good example of great cooperation between the Defence and the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Karnavas. As regard the unsealing of the statement, the Chamber will rule over that issue. Apparently, there will be no difficulty. As far as the second issue is concerned, you've mentioned Oliver Twist. Somebody else mentioned Stevie Wonder. I could also talk about the Judges, the Judges who were also the drafters of the Rules. Of course, it did not escape the Judges' attention, because over the several weeks that we dedicated to several issues, we realised indeed that there was no statement for Defence witnesses. We took a look at the Rules, and the Prosecution has the obligation to provide statements. This obligation is not a Defence's obligation. So you're both right to raise that issue. But after 15 years of existence of that Tribunal, I believe it belonged -- it was up to the various Prosecution teams to raise that issue from the very beginning and not some 15 years later. There is a commission being set up at the moment, a commission which will see how we can speed up the various trials, and I'm sure that this will be part of the agenda of that commission. I read the various summaries, and in particular the summary of that witness statement, and I did realise that there were a lot of things missing. Therefore, I tried to study that summary in order to determine the possible duration of the -- duration of the time to be allotted to the Defence for that particular witness. But with a summary such as this one, it is not enough for me to make such a determination. And Mr. Scott is right in stating his position and in saying that, "It is not on the basis of such a summary that I can work on an equitable basis within this trial." He's right, too, but unfortunately you are not responsible of this state of facts. It is the Judges whom at the very beginning did not realise that such a problem was going to appear. And I said it before and I can repeat it again. If everything had been controlled prior to now, we wouldn't have to have that kind of discussion. Unfortunately, this is too late now. Of course, the Chamber will make a determination because we've been asked to do so by Mr. Scott, and we'll see how we can work this out in the future. But as regards the current witness, it's too late. Now, Mr. Scott complained about documents. I've had a look at the five binders while you were talking, and what did I see? There are four binders containing "P" documents, documents coming from the Prosecution, so the Prosecution of course is very well aware of these documents. It would be quite impossible to think that he isn't. Now, as regards binder number 1, which is the 1D binder, I had a quick look at those documents. I don't need hours to do so. And what did I see? There's a whole bunch of documents which relate to two books which are well known by the Prosecution. It would be unbelievable that the Prosecution didn't know anything about those books. There are several documents relating to the Security Council. There again, it would be quite hard to believe that the Prosecution doesn't know anything about those documents. And there are also some various documents, and there again we don't need hours to understand the content of the documents. So Mr. Scott is saying, "I cannot use those documents to make sure that I can explain my case." I don't agree with him, because I don't think the documents provided by the Defence are unsurmountable. We'll see if we can make a determination and see if from now on we're going to request the Defence teams to provide statements. It's never been done before. It would be quite a revolution in the Tribunal, but sometimes revolutions are useful to take things forward. If we were to determine that from now on, before a Defence witness is heard, we need a statement, a complete, comprehensive statement such as the kind of statements that we request for Prosecution witnesses. Mr. Scott, you're on your feet. Would you like to add anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Perhaps --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I could respond to Mr. Karnavas first, perhaps, and the Chamber's observations, if the counsel might allow me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, as a matter of efficiency that my learned friend alluded to, it just may be more expeditious to respond to the Defence response in toto. He did predicate his remarks as having general application to all Defence teams. So I think it would be more efficient that I be heard, and then of course he should be given proper time to respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm happy to defer to Mr. Khan, Your Honour. That's fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Khan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are three distinction applications put forward by my learned friend. In relation to P 9078, there's no objection at all to the exhibit being made public. Indeed, the Defence starting point is that as much of this trial as possible should be in open session and there should be a very -- Your Honours should be slow in keeping any exhibit confidential unless good cause is shown. In relation to the sufficiency, this was the third point of my learned friend -- in relation to the sufficiency of 65 ter (G) statements, Your Honour, that's a matter between my learned friend Mr. Karnavas and the Trial Chamber, and I don't wish to speak to that. However, I will say that my learned friend Mr. Scott has proposed a definition as to what amounts to a proofing statement. Of course, my learned friend knows very well that the Rules are completely silent as to proofing. There is no public -- as far as I'm aware, no public prosecution guidelines as the probity and proper conduct of what are often called these proofing sessions. They are behind closed doors, there are no transcripts, they're not video-recorded, and they are matters that have had concerns for the Defence in many cases in the past. And, of course, it is a practice that has been frowned upon and prohibited, indeed, by the International Criminal Court. The main submission that has relevance to my -- to the Defence for Bruno Stojic is focused on the Prosecution's submission as to the entitlement to a Defence witness statement and the ostensible prejudice caused to the Prosecution by not having such a statement. My learned friend Mr. Scott is of course a very experienced lawyer with much experience not just in this jurisdiction but in the United States. And of course he knows full well that in the United States not only would he, as a prosecutor, not have access to the name of a Defence witness, he would not have a summary at all or any exhibits at all, and that is something that American prosecutors deal with very familiarly and without any difficulty in many cases indeed. Your Honour has said that, of course, the Tribunal is more than 14 years old.
